title: Phased Commitment Simulator and Composable Lane Playbook (draft)
body:
Context and motivation:

We need a pragmatic approach to letting Dedicated tenants buy/reserve capacity in phases (seasonal/quarterly phasing) while also supporting composable short-term burst lanes, tenant fencing, and graceful soft-quarantine behavior. Many existing drafts focus on one dimension (burst credits, fixed reservations, or preemption). This doc stitches them together into a simulator + playbook that product, infra, and SRE can use to experiment with policy knobs and operational runbooks.

Goals (what success looks like):
- Provide a simulator that models tenant-level commitments, phased ramp-up/down, and short-lived burst lanes so product can evaluate SLA/latency and cost outcomes for realistic workloads.
- Define composable lane primitives (reserve lane, burst lane, opportunistic lane) and a deterministic ordering/priority model for isolation and graceful fallback.
- Produce an operational playbook for tenant fencing, soft quarantine, and rollback windows to minimize noisy-neighbor impact while preserving high customer availability.
- Provide clear metrics to evaluate policies (SLA breach rate, tail latency, percent of burst requests served, warm-start hit rate, and incremental cost).

Assumptions and inputs to the simulator:
- Tenants have one or more reservations with metadata: committed_units (GPU-minutes), phase_windows (date ranges), preferred_region, and fallback_policy.
- There is a global pool of capacity (physical GPUs) with basic fragmentation model; we model warm pools and prewarmed slots.
- Workloads are characterized by arrival distributions (steady vs. spiky), request size distribution (short convo vs. long-generation), and cold-start costs.
- Autoscaler can scale reserved pools +/- 20% within a phase window; burst lanes are ephemeral and draw from opportunistic capacity.
- Latency SLO tiers: gold (p95 < 120ms), silver (p95 < 300ms), bronze (best-effort).

Key primitives and concepts:
- Phase: a time-bounded segment of a reservation that defines baseline capacity and allowed elasticity (e.g., Q4 ramp: commit 60% in Oct, 100% in Nov-Dec).
- Lane: a composable capacity channel with an isolation and priority profile. Types: reserve-lane, burst-lane, opportunistic-lane, prewarm-lane. Lanes can be composed (e.g., a reserve-lane with an attached burst-lane).
- Credit bucket: per-tenant budget for burst consumption. Credits accrue slowly while under-utilized and can be spent to serve bursts. Credits decay if unused (policy knob).
- Tenant fence: a soft isolation boundary that limits cross-tenant interference; represented as a weighted share plus hard circuit-breakers at high utilization.
- Soft quarantine: a controlled degradation mode where problematic tenants are throttled to best-effort lanes while preserving control-plane connectivity and observability.

Simulator design (high level):
- Input: tenant catalog, capacity topology, workload traces (synthetic + sampled production traces).
- Time-step model: 1s steps with event-driven injection; supports simulating weeks of activity with realistic diurnal/weekly patterns.
- Resource allocator: tries ordered lanes for a request (reserve -> burst -> opportunistic). Allocation decisions update local credit buckets, prewarm state, and queue lengths.
- Preemption model: if capacity is exhausted, allocator can evict opportunistic tasks or drain burst allocations per configured preemption priority.
- Metrics emitted: per-tenant latency distribution, unmet requests, burst-credit consumption, eviction count, warm-start hit rate, pod/GPU utilization, cost delta vs. baseline.

Policy knobs to test:
- Phase ramp schedule shapes (linear, logistic, stepped) and their effect on warm pool utilization and latency during ramp events.
- Burst credit accrual and decay rates; max-burst-throttle and per-request credit cost.
- Lane composition: fraction of reserved capacity that is allowed to be borrowed for bursts vs. strictly pinned.
- Tenant fence weights and soft-quarantine thresholds (errors/sec, p99 latency drift, sustained q-length).
- Eviction granularity: slot-level vs. request-level preemption and graceful draining timeouts.

Operational playbook (draft):
1) Pre-ramp validation (2–4 weeks out): run simulator with tenant traces, verify expected warm pool needs, surface tenants with >15% expected p99 regressions and propose targeted prewarm allocations. Link to prewarm runbook PR.
2) Phased ramp gating: for each phase, enable a canary set of tenants to increase commit by 10–20% and validate p95/p99 latencies for 30 min before promoting the phase-wide increase.
3) Burst monitoring: real-time dashboard showing burst-credit consumption, per-tenant burst success rate, and an alert when opportunistic pool utilization > 85% for > 10m.
4) Tenant fence activation: when noisy-neighbor signals (SLO violations) exceed threshold, adjust tenant fence weight to isolate the tenant and shift traffic to best-effort lanes; issue Slack/email to affected customer team.
5) Soft quarantine: if a tenant crosses hard thresholds (error spike, sustained p99 regressions), automatically move new requests to a quarantine lane (rate-limited, logs forwarded). Keep control-plane calls and metrics; require manual review for lift.
6) Rollback: every phase change has an automatic rollback timeout (default 30m). If rollback triggers, we revert lane compositions and signal infra to prewarm for next stable state.

Compatibility notes with existing Redwood features:
- Redwood routing: simulator should model smart routing decisions that prefer local-region reserved lanes and fallback to cross-region opportunistic lanes under capacity pressure.
- Caching + KV prefix reuse: simulate effective per-token compute reduction when prefix caches are hit (reduces burst consumption).
- Reuse existing metrics and tracing hooks so SLO-driven alarms map directly to on-call runbook steps.

SLOs and telemetry to surface:
- Per-tenant: p95, p99, error rate, burst-credit burn rate, percent of requests served from reserve vs opportunistic lanes.
- System: global utilization, number of evictions/min, warm-pool fill ratio, average time-to-fill prewarm.
- Business: incremental cost per served-burst-token, percent of revenue at risk when phases under-serve.

Open questions / tradeoffs to explore in simulator runs:
- Should credits be transferrable across phases (carry-forward) or strictly per-phase? Tradeoff: customer flexibility vs. capacity predictability.
- How aggressive should preemption be during global peaks? Evict opportunistic tasks earlier to protect gold tenants, or prefer throttling new requests?
- Warm pool sizing heuristics: margin sizing vs. dynamic prewarm triggered by short-window forecasts.
- Economic model: reflect committed discounts vs. on-demand burst costs in simulator to quantify customer ROI.

Next steps and experiment plan:
- MVP simulator (week 0–3): ingest historical traces for 10 representative tenants, model basic lanes/credit buckets, run baseline scenarios (steady, seasonal ramp, flash spike).
- Policy matrix (week 3–5): sweep phase shapes x credit policies x preemption strategies; produce a report with recommended defaults for GA.
- Integration (week 6–8): connect simulator to sandbox infra, run live A/B on a small set of tenants with feature flag gated lane composition.
- Docs and runbooks (week 8–10): finalize the operational playbook (SRE + SE signoff) and add Confluence pages + runbook automation.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally implementation-agnostic at first; we want to validate policy spaces before locking into scheduling primitives in the runtime.
- Priority for Q1: reduce tail-latency regressions during seasonal ramps for top 25% revenue tenants.

References and linked artifacts:
- Example traces: s3://redwood-prod-sim/traces/dedicated/top10-tenants-2024-q4.json
- Related PRs: github.com/redwood-inference/ops-playbooks/pull/54
- Existing related docs: reserved-capacity-prioritization-eviction-and-slo-prd-draft.json (see product/dedicated)

Author notes / TODOs:
- Add a short helper script to convert sampled traffic to simulator input formats (Python + pandas).
- Collect feedback from SEs on realistic credit accrual expectations per tenant.
- Validate that the Confluent trace sampler can produce representative long-tail request sizes.
